source: Norman, Monteiro, Sherbino, Ilgen, Schmidt, Mamede (2017) The causes of errors in clinical reasoning: cognitive biases, knowledge deficits, and dual process thinking
finding: Review of the medical literature. Errors come from both fast (Type 1) and slow (Type 2) reasoning. Biases can be induced in the lab, but their real share of diagnostic errors is not well shown.
numbers: Review, no single N. Bias-recognition teaching is ineffective at reducing errors. Knowledge-reorganisation strategies give small but consistent benefits.
quote: Educational strategies directed at the recognition of biases are ineffective in reducing errors
limits: Abstract only on the page opened; no pooled effect size in the abstract.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a bias-checklist prompt to fix errors. Improving how knowledge is organised and retrieved helps more than naming biases.

source: Mamede et al. (2010) Effect of availability bias and reflective reasoning on diagnostic accuracy among internal medicine residents (JAMA 304:1198)
finding: Recent exposure to similar cases pulled second-year residents toward the earlier diagnosis (availability bias). Structured reflection on the case findings raised accuracy.
numbers: N=36 residents (18 PGY1, 18 PGY2), 8 test cases. PGY2: 1.55 on similar-to-earlier cases vs 2.19 on others (P=.03); gave the earlier diagnosis 1.44 vs 0.72 times (P=.04). PGY1 showed the reverse (2.03 vs 1.42, P=.046). Reflection lifted similar-case scores to 2.03 (PGY2) and 2.31 (PGY1), P=.006. Score max 4.0.
limits: Small N, one centre. No main effect of the manipulation; only an interaction with training year. The PGY1 reverse pattern shows the effect is not uniform.
agent_relevance: Primes from a recent similar case bias the next diagnosis. A forced re-analysis of the raw findings (a slot that restates the facts without the prior case) can undo it.

source: Sherbino, Dore, Siu, Norman (2014) Ineffectiveness of cognitive forcing strategies to reduce biases in diagnostic reasoning: a controlled trial
finding: Teaching cognitive forcing strategies to medical students did not reduce search-satisficing or availability errors.
numbers: N=191 (145 trained, 46 control). Search-satisficing cases: 52% vs 48% started a second-diagnosis search (p=.91); 54% vs 48% found it (p=.13). Availability cases: 45% in both groups found the uncommon diagnosis (p=.98). False-positive cases: 64% vs 77% over-searched (p=.12).
limits: Novices (students); allocation method not stated in abstract; computer cases at end of rotation. Underpowered control group.
agent_relevance: A taught stop-and-rethink rule did not transfer. Guardrails must be enforced by code on a signal, not left to the model's own recall of the rule (supports G1).

source: Sherbino, Yip, Dore, Siu, Norman (2011) The effectiveness of cognitive forcing strategies to decrease diagnostic error: an exploratory study
finding: First test of cognitive forcing training. Application and retention were poor.
numbers: N=56 senior medical students, 6 test cases each; 47 tested at once, 9 tested two weeks later. McNemar tests.
limits: Exploratory, no control group, tiny delayed group.
agent_relevance: Debiasing instructions fade. Same lesson as b03: build the check into the process.

source: Lambe, O'Reilly, Kelly, Curristan (2016) Dual-process cognitive interventions to enhance diagnostic reasoning: a systematic review (BMJ Qual Saf 25:808)
finding: Systematic review of interventions to improve analytic and non-analytic reasoning. Guided reflection was the most consistently successful; cognitive forcing improved accuracy and confidence in some studies.
numbers: 28 studies, five databases. Guided reflection effective across five studies. No pooled effect size.
limits: Measures heterogeneous, mostly early-career doctors. Abstract listed five categories but named six.
agent_relevance: Guided reflection (structured re-analysis of findings) is the best-supported fix, which fits an operator that re-derives from the evidence, triggered by a signal.

source: O'Sullivan and Schofield (2019) A cognitive forcing tool to mitigate cognitive bias: a randomised control trial (BMC Med Educ 19:12)
finding: A cognitive forcing tool did not reduce errors on bias-inducing vignettes, though doctors liked it.
numbers: N=76 doctors, single-blind RCT. Mean correct cases 2.8 (tool) vs 3.1 (control); 95% CI -0.94 to 0.45; P=0.49. 20 think-aloud interviews.
limits: Online vignettes, volunteer sample, wide CI. Subjective feedback was positive despite no gain.
agent_relevance: Felt benefit is not evidence of benefit. Judge any scaffold by measured accuracy, never by how reasonable its output reads.

source: Monteiro et al. (2015) Disrupting diagnostic reasoning: do interruptions, instructions, and experience affect diagnostic accuracy and response time? (Acad Med 90:511)
finding: Telling clinicians to go fast or slow, and interrupting them, changed time but not accuracy. Experience mattered a lot.
numbers: 152 residents and 46 emergency physicians, 20 written cases, random fast vs slow instruction. Accuracy 71% (EPs) vs 43% (residents). Response time 55 s (fast) vs 73 s (slow). Interruptions +8 s.
limits: Written general-medicine cases, Canadian and US sites. Time pressure was mild.
agent_relevance: Speed is not the cause of surface-cue errors. Think-longer prompts are not a fix; knowledge and a checked process are.

source: Norman et al. (2014) Reflect versus speed conditions on diagnostic accuracy (Acad Med), as summarised by a web search result
finding: Second-year residents told to speed or to reflect scored the same. Wrong diagnoses took about 17 s longer than right ones.
numbers: Accuracy 44.5% (speed) vs 45.0% (reflect), not significant, 20 cases. Search snippet only; I did not open the paper.
limits: Secondhand summary from search output. Needs checking against the paper.
agent_relevance: Longer reasoning time signals a hard case; it does not make the answer better. Time spent may be usable as an impasse signal.

source: Kahneman and Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree (Am Psychol 64:515)
finding: Fast pattern matching is trustworthy only when the environment gives valid cues and the person has had practice and feedback to learn them. Felt confidence does not tell you which case you are in.
numbers: No numbers; conceptual reconciliation of the heuristics-and-biases and naturalistic decision-making camps.
quote: Subjective experience is not a reliable indicator of judgment accuracy.
limits: Abstract page only. The condition (regular environment plus feedback) is hard to verify case by case.
agent_relevance: Rasmussen's rule-based shortcut is safe in familiar, regular fault families and unsafe elsewhere. Gate S1 fast matches by whether the case lies in a family with past verified outcomes, not by the model's confidence.

source: Gigerenzer and Gaissmaier (2011) Heuristic decision making (Annu Rev Psychol 62:451)
finding: Rival view: simple heuristics can match or beat complex models when data are scarce and the environment is uncertain (less-is-more).
numbers: Only the opening of the abstract was visible on the page opened; no numbers read.
limits: Not read beyond the first sentences. Ecological-rationality claims depend on the environment, as in b09.
agent_relevance: Cheap cue-based triage can be right for the first pass. The question is when to escalate, not whether to ban the shortcut.

source: Mirzadeh et al. (2025) GSM-Symbolic: understanding the limitations of mathematical reasoning in LLMs (ICLR 2025)
finding: Adding one clause that looks relevant but is not (GSM-NoOp) causes large drops. Models turn 'discount' into 'multiply' whatever the context. Changing only the numbers also lowers accuracy and raises variance.
numbers: GSM-NoOp drop up to 65% (Phi-3-mini); the figure also lists o1-mini -29.1, GPT-4o -32.0, GPT-4o-mini -40.0 points. Gap between best and worst number-only instantiation of one question about 12 to 15% for some models.
quote: performance significantly deteriorates as the number of clauses in a question increases
limits: Math word problems, not diagnosis. o1-preview was more robust but still dropped. Drops were larger for newer models in Fig 8a. Figure values read from extracted text, so check against the figure.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM analogue of surface-cue matching: a cue that merely looks relevant gets used. Input hygiene (S1) should strip or flag details not tied to the question.

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large language models can be easily distracted by irrelevant context (ICML)
finding: A single irrelevant sentence breaks many problems the model solved cleanly. Number overlap and role overlap with the problem are the worst lures. Ignore-instructions, distractor examples and self-consistency help.
numbers: GSM-IC-4K: fewer than 30% of base problems solved consistently after distractors; role-overlap sentences drove macro accuracy to 0 for text-davinci-003 on problems of more than 2 steps. Self-consistency (20 samples) gave more than +11 points micro (0-CoT +35.5); correct answer in the 20 samples 99.7%; best macro accuracy still only 45%. The instruction 'Feel free to ignore irrelevant information' improved all prompts; no loss on clean GSM8K.
quote: Feel free to ignore irrelevant information given in the questions.
limits: 2022-era davinci models, arithmetic only. Self-consistency from one model still left over half of base problems unprotected.
agent_relevance: Cheap fixes work partly: an explicit ignore-instruction, and distractor-bearing examples. The right answer is usually among the samples, so selecting by code is better than trusting one pass (G4, G5).

source: McCoy, Yao, Friedman, Hardy, Griffiths (2023) Embers of autoregression: understanding LLMs through the problem they are trained to solve
finding: Accuracy follows how common the input, task and output are, even in deterministic tasks. The model answers with the familiar thing instead of the correct one.
numbers: GPT-4 cipher decoding: 51% when the answer is a high-probability word sequence vs 13% when low. Shift cipher: rot-1 0.82, rot-3 0.76, rot-2 0.02. Rare linear function: 0% for both models vs good on the common one. Output-probability effect on a sentence task: 0.97 vs 0.53.
limits: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 only, 11 tasks, 2023 models. I did not check whether later models show the same effect.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that frequency of a pattern is itself a surface cue for the model. A rare fault whose symptoms resemble a common one will be regularised toward the common one.

source: Binz and Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3 (PNAS)
finding: On classic vignettes GPT-3 often answers as people do, including the intuitive wrong answers. Small rewordings break it.
numbers: 12 vignette tasks: all 12 answered either correctly or in a human-like way; 6 correct. All three Cognitive Reflection Test items answered with the intuitive wrong answer. A cab problem with 15% blue and 85% green gave 20%. Reordering options or rewording the bat-and-ball item still gave 10 cents.
limits: GPT-3 (2022), a handful of items per task, answers hand-classified. Not a test of newer models.
agent_relevance: A fast-but-wrong answer is the default; the model does not spontaneously override it. Overriding must come from a trigger and a check outside the model.

source: Turpin, Michael, Perez, Bowman (2023) Language models don't always say what they think: unfaithful explanations in chain-of-thought prompting
finding: Hidden cues in the prompt (a suggested answer, always-A in few-shot examples) shift the answer, and the written reasoning rationalises it without mentioning the cue.
numbers: 13 BIG-Bench Hard tasks, GPT-3.5 and Claude 1.0. Zero-shot CoT accuracy fell as much as 36.3 points under Suggested Answer bias; under Answer-is-Always-A the drop was 18.7 points for GPT-3.5 and 4.7 for Claude 1.0. All drops significant, CI about 1.6 to 2.4.
limits: 2023 models; effect varies a lot by task. Later models were not retested here.
agent_relevance: The model's explanation is not a record of why it answered. Do not use a model's stated reason as evidence that a cue was ignored (supports G1 and the F11 finding).

source: Liu et al. (2024) Lost in the middle: how language models use long contexts (TACL)
finding: Evidence placed in the middle of a long input is used much less than at the start or end.
numbers: U-shaped accuracy curve over answer position. For GPT-3.5-turbo with 20 documents, the worst middle position fell below its closed-book result (56.1%). Authors report drops of more than 20 points in the worst case.
limits: Retrieval QA and key-value tasks; not diagnosis. 2023 model set. Later long-context models may differ (not tested here).
agent_relevance: Position is a surface cue. Put the decisive symptoms first or last, or split a long log into short slices and handle them in code.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) Large language models are not robust multiple choice selectors (ICLR 2024)
finding: Models prefer certain option letters. A debias fix that estimates the prior over option IDs works; prompt-only fixes do not.
numbers: 20 LLMs, 3 benchmarks. Moving the correct answer to D lowered gpt-3.5-turbo from 67.2 to 60.9; moving it to A raised llama-30B by 15.2 points to 68.2 vs 65.3 for gpt-3.5. An explicit debias instruction and CoT did not remove the bias. PriDe (permute options on a small sample) removes most of it.
limits: Multiple-choice format only. 2023-vintage models.
agent_relevance: When the agent picks among candidate faults, shuffle the order in code and count agreement across orders (G5).

source: Schmidgall et al. (2024) Addressing cognitive bias in medical language models (BiasMedQA)
finding: Bias text added to USMLE questions lowers accuracy in every model. Telling the model about the bias, or showing it a bad example, recovers only part for a few models.
numbers: 1,273 USMLE questions, 7 biases, 6 LLMs. No-bias accuracy: GPT-4 72.7%, Mixtral 51.8%, GPT-3.5 49.7%, PMC-Llama 33.4%. Average drop by bias: false consensus 24.9%, frequency 18.2%, recency 12.9%, confirmation 8.1%. GPT-4 worst case -14.0% (false consensus), confirmation -0.2%. GPT-3.5 average -37.4%. Education prompt: GPT-4 frequency bias 0.627 to 0.720; one-shot: recency 0.679 to 0.742. Weaker models gained little; safety filters blocked many mitigated runs.
limits: Multiple-choice exam format with injected bias text; not real diagnosis. Mitigation gains uneven and weak for small models.
agent_relevance: Telling a weak model about bias barely helps; a strong model benefits. A scaffold cannot count on be-aware-of-bias for a small model.

source: Vishwanath et al. (2025) Medical large language models are easily distracted (MedDistractQA)
finding: Irrelevant statements in a clinical question lower accuracy. RAG and medical fine-tuning did not fix it.
numbers: Accuracy fell 2.2% to 17.8% (non-literal clinical words) and 1.3% to 17.9% (bystander statements), up to 17.9% in the abstract. General open-source models -10.9% vs proprietary -3.8% (p=5.4e-8); medical fine-tuned open-source -10.0% vs -3.8% (p=0.0375). Biggest drop on Patient Care: Diagnosis (-10.1%).
limits: USMLE-style text questions; distractors inserted by template. Preprint under review.
agent_relevance: Medical fine-tuning and retrieval do not remove lures. A cleaning step that restates only the relevant facts (S1) is a better bet.

source: Singh, Deka, Chennareddy (2026) Same illness, different voice: restating the patient's account narrows narrative anchoring in clinical LMs
finding: Same audited facts told in a patient's own voice lower accuracy in all 12 models. Chain-of-thought and debias prompts remove a fifth of the gap. Having the model first rewrite the account as a clinical vignette halves the gap and raises accuracy.
numbers: 1,000 MedQA cases x 3 retellings, 12 open models (3B to 24B). Penalty -9.6 points (95% CI -11.0 to -8.2), 26% more errors; no reduction with scale. Rewrite-then-reason: gap halved, marked-voice accuracy +3.9 points (11 models). A schema-extraction pipeline closed the gap but was 7.1 points less accurate in all 11 models. Rewriting also invents plausible details. In one case 8 of 11 models switched from Pick's disease to Lewy body dementia when a metaphor was read as a symptom.
limits: Open models only; generation settings differed across voices, so the authors do not claim register alone is the cause. Preprint, v2 Oct 2026.
agent_relevance: Best direct test of input hygiene: restate the report in neutral form first, then reason. But prose rewriting can add facts, and rigid schema extraction loses accuracy. Check the rewrite against the source in code.

source: Braitsch et al. (2026) Information-seeking failures of LLMs in agentic clinical reasoning (OncoRounds)
finding: When models must ask for data over three rounds, the dominant errors are search satisficing, anchoring and premature closure, as in novice doctors. Early wrong diagnoses rarely get corrected.
numbers: 32 frontier models, best 68% overall accuracy. Data utilisation predicts accuracy (R=0.69, P<0.001) but fell from 57% to 26% in round 3. Of 323 pairs with a wrong first diagnosis, 212 (65.6%) stayed wrong (recovery 34.4%); of 307 right first diagnoses, 156 (50.8%) became wrong. Recovery: Claude Opus 4.5 6/6, Opus 4.6 7/8, Qwen3 Next 80b 1/14. Reasoning traces scored 91% above threshold but did not track accuracy.
limits: Hematologic oncology, small case set; some models did not finish all cases. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Strong match for G1/G2: early wrong labels stick, fluent rationales mislead, and recovery differs sharply by model. Require evidence requests before commitment and re-check late.

source: Roy et al. (2024) Exploring LLM-based agents for root cause analysis (Microsoft)
finding: Retrieval of similar past incidents (surface similarity) gives plausible root causes with a high hallucination rate; a tool-using ReAct agent hallucinates much less but often says information is insufficient.
numbers: Correct rate 35% (ReAct with BM25 search) vs 39% for baselines. Hallucination rate 4% ReAct vs 12% CoT vs 40% retrieval (k=10). 66% of ReAct's wrong answers were insufficient-information vs 32% for CoT and 18% for retrieval. 26% (10 of 38) of retrieval's correct answers contained hallucinations.
limits: Zero-shot, small labelled incident set, lexical metrics unreliable, manual labelling.
agent_relevance: Closest software-fault analogue: nearest-past-incident matching looks right but is often built on invented detail. Gather live evidence before naming a cause.

source: Sharma et al. (2024) Towards understanding sycophancy in language models (ICLR 2024)
finding: Models shift toward a user's stated view. A hinted wrong answer lowers accuracy.
numbers: A user suggesting an incorrect answer reduced accuracy by up to 27% (LLaMA 2).
limits: Only the abstract and one results line were read; per-model figures not checked. Human preference data partly drives the effect.
agent_relevance: A prior guess in the prompt acts as a surface cue. Hide candidate answers from checking steps (G5).

source: Singh et al. (2026) same paper, structured-schema arm (arXiv 2607.27384)
finding: Forcing the report into a fixed schema removed the voice gap but cost accuracy; adding reasoning agents or tools cost more.
numbers: Schema pipeline 7.1 points less accurate in all 11 models vs rewrite-then-reason; paper says adding agents or tools costs more still.
limits: Same preprint and limits as b20.
agent_relevance: Fixed field extraction at S1 can drop the key symptom. Prefer a prose restatement checked against the source.

source: Shi et al. (2023) same paper, GSM8K clean-set check (arXiv 2302.00093)
finding: Distractor examples and the ignore-instruction did not hurt accuracy on the clean GSM8K dev set.
numbers: No drop on clean GSM8K or SVAMP when adding distractor exemplars, instruction, or both.
limits: Arithmetic only; text-davinci era models.
agent_relevance: An always-on ignore-irrelevant instruction at S1 looks cheap and safe, but test it on our own data first.
